default.title: Architecture Design
default.heroHeading: Architecture that belongs to its place.
default.shortDescription: Concept, planning and detailing for homes and commercial buildings — resolved against the site, the brief and the way the building has to be built.
default.description: Every project begins with the site and the people who will use it. We work through orientation, light, circulation and structure until the plan is doing real work, then develop the elevations, materials and details that give the building its character. The drawings that leave the studio are made to be built from.

heroImage.alt: Modern house of layered dark and timber volumes set behind a mature tree

indexImage.alt: Dark-clad residential facade with a timber-lined entrance lit from within

sections.label: Concept & Planning
sections.heading: Reading the site before drawing the building.
sections.body: Before anything is designed we establish what the site will allow and what the brief actually asks for — approach and access, orientation and prevailing light, the shape of the plot, the budget direction the design has to respect.

image.alt: Overhead view of a low-rise residential neighbourhood, plots read as a plan

sections.label: Architectural Design
sections.heading: Plan, section and elevation, developed together.
sections.body: Concepts are tested in plan and section at the same time, so that spatial planning, structure and elevation move as one idea rather than three separate exercises.

image.alt: Close study of a facade's repeating angled fins catching raking daylight

sections.label: Design Development
sections.heading: Drawn to the level the site needs.
sections.body: Design development is where a scheme becomes buildable — dimensioned plans, sections through the tricky parts, elevations that resolve, and material studies that settle questions before they reach the site.

image.alt: Architect marking up a set of rolled construction drawings at a timber desk

sections.label: Project Coordination
sections.heading: Holding the intent through to execution.
sections.body: Drawings only matter if what gets built follows them. We stay involved through execution so that decisions made on site are made against the design, not around it.

image.alt: Supervision team walking a freshly poured slab across a large construction site

default.title: Interior Design
default.heroHeading: Interiors designed around how spaces are lived.
default.shortDescription: Residential and commercial interiors resolved from space planning through to material, lighting and the detail of every joint.
default.description: Interiors are planned before they are decorated. We start with how a room is entered, crossed and used at different times of day, then work outward into layouts, materials, lighting and the custom pieces that make a space specific to the people in it.

heroImage.alt: Open-plan living room with a full-height timber wall and a pale sectional sofa

indexImage.alt: Living room opening to a garden through full-height doors, with low seating and clay-toned tables

sections.label: Residential Interiors
sections.heading: Rooms that hold up to daily use.
sections.body: Family homes have to work early in the morning and late at night. Planning accounts for storage, circulation between rooms, natural light and the quiet spaces a household needs.

image.alt: Sitting room lit by woven rattan pendants above a grey sofa and patterned rug

sections.label: Commercial Interiors
sections.heading: Workspaces, retail and hospitality.
sections.body: Commercial interiors carry a different set of demands — throughput, servicing, brand presence and the wear that comes from constant use.

image.alt: Workspace lounge with tan chairs on polished concrete inside a full-height glazed corner

sections.label: Materials & Detail
sections.heading: Chosen in the room, not from a catalogue.
sections.body: Material selection is tested against the light the space actually gets. Colour, texture and finish are decided together, then carried through into the detailing so the built result matches the drawing.

default.title: Vastu Consultancy
default.heroHeading: Thoughtful spaces, aligned with the way they are meant to work.
default.shortDescription: Spatial planning informed by Vastu principles — orientation, entrance, circulation and room placement, integrated into the architecture rather than applied over it.
default.description: We treat Vastu as a planning discipline: a set of principles about orientation, sequence and placement that can be resolved inside a working architectural plan. Guidance is given in drawings — site orientation, entry, circulation and room placement — and integrated with the design rather than layered on afterwards.

heroImage.alt: Repeating white arches receding along a daylit corridor above a broad flight of steps

indexImage.alt: Arched opening framing a low dark sofa in a pale, near-empty room

sections.label: Site & Orientation
sections.heading: Starting from the plot and its directions.
sections.body: Orientation is established against the plot itself — the approach, the road, the surrounding built edge and the path of the sun across the site through the year.

image.alt: Overhead view of a low-rise residential neighbourhood, plots read as a plan

sections.label: Spatial Planning
sections.heading: Principles resolved inside a working plan.
sections.body: Guidance only holds if the plan still functions. Zones are arranged so that the placement principles and the practical requirements of the household are satisfied by the same layout.

sections.label: Entrance & Circulation
sections.heading: The sequence of arrival.
sections.body: Where a building is entered sets how it is understood. We work through the entrance position, the threshold and the route from it into the main spaces.

image.alt: Street elevation of a house where a timber-clad volume folds over the entrance gate

sections.label: Room Placement
sections.heading: Placing the rooms that matter most.
sections.body: Kitchen, bedrooms, pooja space, storage and services are positioned against the directional framework and against the daylight and privacy each one needs.

image.alt: Arched opening framing a low dark sofa in a pale, near-empty room

sections.label: Existing Property Assessment
sections.heading: Reviewing a building already standing.
sections.body: For an existing home or premises we review the current plan against the principles and set out what can be adjusted — and what would require structural change to alter.

image.alt: Interior stripped back to studs and masonry during renovation, with a doorway cut through

sections.label: Design Integration
sections.heading: Carried into the drawings.
sections.body: Recommendations are issued as marked plans so they travel with the rest of the drawing set into design development and execution.

image.alt: Architect marking up a set of rolled construction drawings at a timber desk

default.title: Construction
default.heroHeading: From drawing board to built form.
default.shortDescription: Structural execution, civil work and finishing carried out against the drawing set, with the design team present through the build.
default.description: Construction is where the design is either kept or lost. We run the build against the same drawings we produced — setting out, structure, civil work and finishing — with supervision on site so that detail decisions are resolved against the design intent.

heroImage.alt: Reinforcement bar being tied across a suspended slab by workers on site

indexImage.alt: Workers fixing reinforcement to columns on a rising concrete frame

sections.label: Pre-Construction
sections.heading: Setting out before the first pour.
sections.body: Levels, setting out, sequencing and material scheduling are established from the drawings so that the sequence of work is agreed before it begins.

image.alt: Architect marking up a set of rolled construction drawings at a timber desk

sections.label: Structural Execution
sections.heading: Frame, reinforcement and slab.
sections.body: Foundations, columns, beams and slabs executed to the structural drawings, with reinforcement and formwork checked before each pour.

image.alt: Workers fixing reinforcement to columns on a rising concrete frame

sections.label: Civil Work
sections.heading: Masonry, plaster and services routing.
sections.body: Brickwork, blockwork, plaster, waterproofing and the routing of services are coordinated so that later finishing work is not chasing earlier decisions.

image.alt: Supervision team walking a freshly poured slab across a large construction site

sections.label: Finishing
sections.heading: Where the tolerances get tight.
sections.body: Flooring, joinery, painting, fixtures and fittings — the stage where the difference between adequate and well-built becomes visible.

image.alt: Site worker in a hard hat carrying out finishing work against an external wall

sections.label: Site Coordination
sections.heading: One team across design and build.
sections.body: Because the design and build sit under one studio, questions raised on site are answered against the drawings rather than negotiated between separate parties.

default.title: Renovation
default.heroHeading: Give existing spaces a new direction.
default.shortDescription: Reworking homes, interiors and facades that are already standing — reconfiguring space, upgrading finishes and bringing tired buildings back into use.
default.description: Renovation starts by understanding what is already there: what is structural, what can move, and what is worth keeping. From that we plan the reconfiguration, the upgrades and the sequence of work needed to get from the existing building to the intended one.

heroImage.alt: Interior stripped back to studs and masonry during renovation, with a doorway cut through

indexImage.alt: Bathroom lined in large-format grey stone with a timber vanity and freestanding tub

sections.label: Assessment
sections.heading: Understanding what can move.
sections.body: A survey of the existing structure establishes which walls are load-bearing, where services run, and what the building will allow before any new layout is drawn.

sections.label: Space Reconfiguration
sections.heading: A better plan out of the same footprint.
sections.body: Most renovations gain more from a rearranged plan than from new finishes. Openings, circulation and room boundaries are reconsidered first.

image.alt: Double-height living space with a light timber stair rising against white walls

sections.label: Interior & Finishing Upgrades
sections.heading: Kitchens, bathrooms and surfaces.
sections.body: Concentrated upgrades to the rooms that carry the most daily use, planned so that the work can be staged around the household where needed.

image.alt: Kitchen island in veined stone with a patterned splashback behind the range

sections.label: Facade Renovation
sections.heading: Changing how a building presents itself.
sections.body: External work — re-cladding, new openings, screening and weathering repairs — that resets a building's presence on its street.

image.alt: Street elevation of a house where a timber-clad volume folds over the entrance gate

sections.heading: Workspaces, retail and hospitality.
sections.body: Commercial interiors carry a different set of demands — throughput, servicing, brand presence and the wear that comes from constant use.

image.alt: Workspace lounge with tan chairs on polished concrete inside a full-height glazed corner

sections.heading: Chosen in the room, not from a catalogue.
sections.body: Material selection is tested against the light the space actually gets. Colour, texture and finish are decided together, then carried through into the detailing so the built result matches the drawing.

services.title: Vastu Consultancy
services.heroHeading: Thoughtful spaces, aligned with the way they are meant to work.
services.shortDescription: Spatial planning informed by Vastu principles — orientation, entrance, circulation and room placement, integrated into the architecture rather than applied over it.
services.description: We treat Vastu as a planning discipline: a set of principles about orientation, sequence and placement that can be resolved inside a working architectural plan. Guidance is given in drawings — site orientation, entry, circulation and room placement — and integrated with the design rather than layered on afterwards.

heroImage.alt: Repeating white arches receding along a daylit corridor above a broad flight of steps

indexImage.alt: Arched opening framing a low dark sofa in a pale, near-empty room

sections.label: Site & Orientation
sections.heading: Starting from the plot and its directions.
sections.body: Orientation is established against the plot itself — the approach, the road, the surrounding built edge and the path of the sun across the site through the year.

image.alt: Overhead view of a low-rise residential neighbourhood, plots read as a plan

sections.label: Spatial Planning
sections.heading: Principles resolved inside a working plan.
sections.body: Guidance only holds if the plan still functions. Zones are arranged so that the placement principles and the practical requirements of the household are satisfied by the same layout.

sections.label: Entrance & Circulation
sections.heading: The sequence of arrival.
sections.body: Where a building is entered sets how it is understood. We work through the entrance position, the threshold and the route from it into the main spaces.

image.alt: Street elevation of a house where a timber-clad volume folds over the entrance gate

sections.label: Room Placement
sections.heading: Placing the rooms that matter most.
sections.body: Kitchen, bedrooms, pooja space, storage and services are positioned against the directional framework and against the daylight and privacy each one needs.

image.alt: Arched opening framing a low dark sofa in a pale, near-empty room

sections.label: Existing Property Assessment
sections.heading: Reviewing a building already standing.
sections.body: For an existing home or premises we review the current plan against the principles and set out what can be adjusted — and what would require structural change to alter.

image.alt: Interior stripped back to studs and masonry during renovation, with a doorway cut through

sections.label: Design Integration
sections.heading: Carried into the drawings.
sections.body: Recommendations are issued as marked plans so they travel with the rest of the drawing set into design development and execution.

image.alt: Architect marking up a set of rolled construction drawings at a timber desk

services.title: Construction
services.heroHeading: From drawing board to built form.
services.shortDescription: Structural execution, civil work and finishing carried out against the drawing set, with the design team present through the build.
services.description: Construction is where the design is either kept or lost. We run the build against the same drawings we produced — setting out, structure, civil work and finishing — with supervision on site so that detail decisions are resolved against the design intent.

heroImage.alt: Reinforcement bar being tied across a suspended slab by workers on site

indexImage.alt: Workers fixing reinforcement to columns on a rising concrete frame

sections.label: Pre-Construction
sections.heading: Setting out before the first pour.
sections.body: Levels, setting out, sequencing and material scheduling are established from the drawings so that the sequence of work is agreed before it begins.

image.alt: Architect marking up a set of rolled construction drawings at a timber desk

sections.label: Structural Execution
sections.heading: Frame, reinforcement and slab.
sections.body: Foundations, columns, beams and slabs executed to the structural drawings, with reinforcement and formwork checked before each pour.

image.alt: Workers fixing reinforcement to columns on a rising concrete frame

sections.label: Civil Work
sections.heading: Masonry, plaster and services routing.
sections.body: Brickwork, blockwork, plaster, waterproofing and the routing of services are coordinated so that later finishing work is not chasing earlier decisions.

image.alt: Supervision team walking a freshly poured slab across a large construction site

sections.label: Finishing
sections.heading: Where the tolerances get tight.
sections.body: Flooring, joinery, painting, fixtures and fittings — the stage where the difference between adequate and well-built becomes visible.

image.alt: Site worker in a hard hat carrying out finishing work against an external wall

sections.label: Site Coordination
sections.heading: One team across design and build.
sections.body: Because the design and build sit under one studio, questions raised on site are answered against the drawings rather than negotiated between separate parties.

services.title: Renovation
services.heroHeading: Give existing spaces a new direction.
services.shortDescription: Reworking homes, interiors and facades that are already standing — reconfiguring space, upgrading finishes and bringing tired buildings back into use.
services.description: Renovation starts by understanding what is already there: what is structural, what can move, and what is worth keeping. From that we plan the reconfiguration, the upgrades and the sequence of work needed to get from the existing building to the intended one.

heroImage.alt: Interior stripped back to studs and masonry during renovation, with a doorway cut through

indexImage.alt: Bathroom lined in large-format grey stone with a timber vanity and freestanding tub

sections.label: Assessment
sections.heading: Understanding what can move.
sections.body: A survey of the existing structure establishes which walls are load-bearing, where services run, and what the building will allow before any new layout is drawn.

sections.label: Space Reconfiguration
sections.heading: A better plan out of the same footprint.
sections.body: Most renovations gain more from a rearranged plan than from new finishes. Openings, circulation and room boundaries are reconsidered first.

image.alt: Double-height living space with a light timber stair rising against white walls

sections.label: Interior & Finishing Upgrades
sections.heading: Kitchens, bathrooms and surfaces.
sections.body: Concentrated upgrades to the rooms that carry the most daily use, planned so that the work can be staged around the household where needed.

image.alt: Kitchen island in veined stone with a patterned splashback behind the range

sections.label: Facade Renovation
sections.heading: Changing how a building presents itself.
sections.body: External work — re-cladding, new openings, screening and weathering repairs — that resets a building's presence on its street.

default.title: Courtyard House
default.shortDescription: A family home planned inward around a central court, so that every principal room borrows light and air from the same open middle.
default.description: The plot is deep and narrow, hemmed in on both long sides. Rather than push the house to one edge, the plan opens a court at its centre and arranges the living spaces around it. Circulation runs along the court, which means the corridor is daylit for its full length and the rooms on either side face a quiet, private outlook rather than a boundary wall.

coverImage.alt: Modern house of layered dark and timber volumes set behind a mature tree

default.designIntent: Every deep plot in the neighbourhood resolves the same problem differently. Here the answer was to give the house a middle — a court that the plan can turn towards, so the deepest rooms are no longer the darkest.
default.spatialPlanning: Public rooms occupy the ground level around three sides of the court, with the fourth left open to the garden. Bedrooms sit above, set back on the court side to keep sightlines between levels indirect.
default.interiorNote: Interiors are kept quiet so the court remains the event. Timber is used at the points the hand meets the building — doors, rails, joinery — and the wall surfaces stay plain.
default.constructionNote: A reinforced concrete frame allowed the court elevations to be almost entirely glazed, with the structure pulled back behind the line of the opening.
default.outcomeNote: The house reads as a single volume from the street and opens completely once inside it.

default.title: Screened Residence
default.shortDescription: A perforated screen wraps the western elevation, cutting afternoon heat without closing the house off from its garden.
default.description: The site's best outlook and its worst sun arrive from the same direction. A deep perforated screen set forward of the glazing resolves both: the view survives, the glare does not, and the gap between the screen and the wall becomes a shaded service edge.

coverImage.alt: Perforated screen wall filtering light across a poolside elevation

default.designIntent: Shading is treated as architecture rather than as an attachment. The screen sets the proportion of the elevation and the rhythm of everything behind it.
default.spatialPlanning: Entry, kitchen and principal bedroom placement were resolved against the directional framework agreed at the Vastu stage and then held through design development.
default.interiorNote: The screen throws a moving pattern across the internal floors through the afternoon, which set the decision to keep those floors pale and unfigured.
default.constructionNote: The screen is a separate frame tied back to the slab edges, so it could be set out and installed independently of the main envelope.
default.outcomeNote: A west-facing house that stays usable through the hottest part of the day.

Sweeping white facade clad in a fine perforated diagrid panel system

default.title: Terrace Apartment
default.shortDescription: An interior fit-out that removes two internal walls and lets one continuous living space run the width of the apartment.
default.description: The original plan divided the front of the apartment into three small rooms, none of which worked hard. Taking out two non-structural partitions produced a single space that runs from the kitchen to the terrace doors, with the functions separated by joinery and level rather than by walls.

coverImage.alt: Sitting room lit by woven rattan pendants above a grey sofa and patterned rug

default.designIntent: Fewer rooms, better rooms. The gain here was in removal, not addition.
default.spatialPlanning: A long joinery wall absorbs storage, services and the television, which let every other surface in the room stay clear.
default.interiorNote: Warm neutrals, woven light fittings and a single dark anchor piece per zone. Nothing in the palette competes with the terrace planting.
default.constructionNote: Partition removal was carried out after a structural check confirmed both walls were non-load-bearing.
default.outcomeNote: A flat that now reads as one bright room facing the terrace.

default.title: Workshop Offices

default.designIntent: Build the fixed things well and leave the rest adjustable.
default.spatialPlanning: Cellular rooms line the solid edge; open desking sits along the glazed edge; the spine between them carries circulation and shared functions.
default.interiorNote: Polished concrete, black steel and a single warm timber note at the meeting rooms.
default.constructionNote: Services were coordinated on the drawings before installation, which kept the exposed ceiling legible rather than crowded.
default.outcomeNote: An office that can be replanned in a weekend.

Compact study with a timber desk against a deep green wall beside a bright window

default.title: Riverside Villa
default.shortDescription: A long, low house set across the slope of its site, holding the view in one direction and privacy in the other.
default.description: The site falls gently towards open ground. The house is set along the contour rather than across it, which keeps the earthworks light and gives every principal room the same outlook. The approach side is deliberately closed.

coverImage.alt: Modern villa with a cantilevered upper floor overlooking a swimming pool

default.spatialPlanning: A single-loaded corridor along the closed edge serves all the main rooms, so nothing occupies the view frontage except the rooms that deserve it.
default.interiorNote: Interiors are still in development. Material direction is set towards stone floors and lime-finished walls.
default.constructionNote: Currently in structural execution. Frame and slabs are complete to the upper level.

default.title: Brick House Renovation
default.shortDescription: A tired family house stripped back to its sound structure, replanned and refinished without extending its footprint.
default.description: Nothing was added to the outside of this house. The work was internal: partitions removed, openings enlarged, services replaced and the wet rooms rebuilt. What the plan gained in openness it kept in structure.

coverImage.alt: Interior stripped back to studs and masonry during renovation, with a doorway cut through

default.designIntent: The building was sound. What it needed was a better plan and honest finishes.
default.spatialPlanning: The ground floor was reduced from six rooms to four, with the kitchen brought forward to the garden side.
default.interiorNote: Existing brickwork was retained and left visible in the stair hall as a record of what the house had been.
default.constructionNote: Work was staged so the upper floor stayed habitable while the ground floor was rebuilt.
default.outcomeNote: Same footprint, an entirely different house to live in.

default.title: Garden Pavilion
default.shortDescription: A small freestanding structure at the end of an existing garden — one room, four openings and a deep overhanging roof.
default.description: A single-room pavilion used for work and for gathering. The roof oversails on all four sides so the space can stay open through most of the year, and the walls are little more than the frame between the openings.

coverImage.alt: Arched opening framing a low dark sofa in a pale, near-empty room

default.designIntent: At this scale everything is a detail. The roof edge does most of the work.
default.spatialPlanning: One room, sited at the far corner of the garden so the walk to it is part of the point.
default.interiorNote: A plain lime-washed interior, deliberately unfurnished beyond what the room needs.
default.constructionNote: A steel frame with masonry infill, which kept the corners open and the roof edge thin.
default.outcomeNote: The most-used room on the property.

default.title: Planning for light before planning for rooms

coverImage.alt: Repeating white arches receding along a daylit corridor above a broad flight of steps

default.excerpt: On deep plots the darkest room is usually the one nobody planned for. Starting from where the light lands changes the plan that follows.
body: The standard way to plan a house is to list the rooms and then fit them to the plot. It is fast, and on a generous site it works. On the deep, narrow plots common across Lucknow it produces the same result every time: a bright front, a bright back, and a dead middle nobody wants to use.

The alternative is to establish where daylight can reach before deciding what goes where. That usually means opening a court, a light well or a double-height slot somewhere in the body of the plan, and accepting that the built area lost is smaller than the usable area gained.

Once the light is placed, circulation should follow it. A corridor along a court is a daylit corridor, and the rooms it serves face something other than a boundary wall. The plan does more work for the same footprint.

default.title: Reading a site before you draw

coverImage.alt: Overhead view of a low-rise residential neighbourhood, plots read as a plan

default.excerpt: Orientation, approach, prevailing wind and the built edge around a plot decide more about a building than most briefs do.
body: A site visit that only measures the plot has missed most of the information. What matters as much as the dimensions is where the sun crosses, which direction carries the afternoon heat, where the noise comes from, and what is likely to be built next door.

Those constraints usually point towards a plan before any drawing starts. A west elevation that has to be shaded, an approach that has to be turned, a neighbour who will eventually build up to the boundary — each of these removes options, which is useful.
By the time the first sketch is made, a well-read site has already answered several questions that would otherwise be settled by preference.

default.title: Vastu as a planning discipline

coverImage.alt: Arched opening framing a low dark sofa in a pale, near-empty room

default.excerpt: Treated as a set of principles about orientation, sequence and placement, Vastu resolves inside a working plan rather than fighting it.
body: Vastu guidance is often received as a list of rules delivered after a plan already exists, which is the hardest possible point to apply it. Introduced at the start, it behaves like any other planning constraint: it narrows the options and makes the remaining choices clearer.

The principles that most often shape a plan concern orientation, the position of the entrance, the sequence of arrival, and the placement of the kitchen, the pooja space and the principal bedroom. All of these are spatial decisions, and all of them are easier to satisfy while the plan is still loose.

Where a requirement and a practical constraint genuinely conflict, that should be discussed openly rather than resolved silently in one direction. What we do not do is make claims about outcomes — the discipline here is spatial, and we keep it there.

default.title: The case for fewer materials

coverImage.alt: Detail of a glazed brick-bond splashback meeting an oak counter and undermount sink

default.excerpt: A short palette, used consistently, reads as considered. A long one reads as indecision, however good each individual choice was.
body: Most interiors improve when the material list gets shorter. Three or four surfaces repeated across a house give it coherence; a different floor in every room gives it none, regardless of the quality of any single floor.
A short palette also survives the build better. Fewer materials means fewer trades, fewer junctions to detail, and fewer opportunities for a substitution on site to break the intent.
The discipline is in the junctions rather than the selections. Where two materials meet is where the quality of a room is actually decided.

default.title: What a renovation survey should establish

coverImage.alt: Interior stripped back to studs and masonry during renovation, with a doorway cut through

default.excerpt: Before a single new layout is drawn, four things about the existing building need to be known with certainty.
body: Which walls carry load. Where the services run. What condition the roof and the wet areas are actually in. And what the building was originally built from — because that determines what can be cut, chased or removed.
Renovations go wrong when a plan is drawn against assumptions and corrected on site. Every correction made after demolition has started costs more than the survey that would have prevented it.
A good survey typically shortens the design stage rather than extending it, because it removes the options that were never available.

default.title: Detailing for the people who build it

coverImage.alt: Site worker in a hard hat carrying out finishing work against an external wall

default.excerpt: A drawing that cannot be built from is not finished, however well it reads on screen.
body: The test of a detail is whether the person holding the drawing on site can build it in the sequence the site is actually working in. A junction that requires three trades to be present simultaneously is a detail that will be improvised.
That is an argument for staying involved through execution. Questions raised at the wall are answered fastest by the people who drew it, and answered against the design rather than around it.
It is also an argument for drawing less, but drawing the right things. The details that matter are the ones that repeat and the ones that are hard.

founder.heading: Why we work this way.
message: Most of what goes wrong on a building site was decided months earlier, on paper, by someone who was never going to be there when it was built. A detail gets drawn one way and priced another. A question comes up at the wall on a Tuesday and gets answered by whoever is standing closest.

We set the studio up to close that gap. The same people who read the site and drew the plan are the people coordinating the build, which means a decision made on site is made against the design rather than around it. It is a slower way to start a project and a considerably faster way to finish one.

If you are planning something — a house, a workplace, a renovation of a building you already own — tell us about the site before you tell us about the brief. The plot usually answers half the questions on its own.
